title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hook: on Shivaratri the kitchen doesn't close, it changes, and hunger becomes a bell that keeps ringing

segments.voice: Yesterday, lesson one of Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum: the sankalpa, a resolve made in daylight with water in the palm. Did you keep your small resolve when the moment to quit came? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.
screen: `THE SANKALPA, MADE IN DAYLIGHT.` · `THE WEEK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: On the day of Shivaratri, in some kitchens, the stove is still on. The food has just changed. No rice, no wheat, no lentils. Instead, a pan of sago pearls softening with potato and crushed peanuts, a bowl of fruit, a glass of milk. In other homes, nothing goes on the stove at all, and people take only water until the next morning. Different vows, different tables. But in each version, at some point in the afternoon, the stomach speaks up. It speaks up again in the evening, and again around midnight. Today's lesson in the night curriculum is that voice. Not how to silence it. What to do with it when it rings.
screen: `THE KITCHEN CHANGES.` → `DIFFERENT VOWS, DIFFERENT TABLES.` → `THE STOMACH SPEAKS UP.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word for a fast is upavasa. Some teachers hear in it the sense of staying near, and they read the fast that way: not as going without, but as keeping close to the one the night is for. Look at what a fast actually does on this night. First, it clears space. No meals to cook, serve and clean up means hours handed back, and the vow spends them on worship. Second, it turns hunger into a bell. Every pang is a small interruption, and on Shivaratri each interruption can be met with the same question: why am I awake? The body keeps ringing, and the ringing keeps calling the mind home. Third, a fast is held inside a vow, not inside a punishment. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, and it isn't for the one who doesn't eat at all. So a household keeping Shivaratri can make room for children, for the sick, and for anyone a fast would hurt. A glass of milk taken honestly under the vow is still the vow. Now look back at the week. It began inside the Rudram, bowing to the short and the tall, to trees and foam, then turning to ask, and to me. We left it chanted as water poured over the stone. Then the night opened: its shape, then the morning resolve, and now the fast. The pattern runs all the way through. A fierce thing, met with a bow. A long night, met with a promise. Hunger, met with a question. Each time, something hard is not avoided. It's turned into attention.
screen: `UPAVASA: STAYING NEAR.` · `A FAST CLEARS SPACE.` · `HUNGER BECOMES A BELL.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT NONE AT ALL.` · then, large: `THE HARD THING BECOMES ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use a small want as a bell. Settle, and breathe. Sooner or later in this sit, something will tug at you: an itch, a thought of food, the urge to check a message. Don't act on it, and don't fight it. When it rings, ask yourself quietly: why am I sitting here? Then come back to the breath. Each tug is one more ring of the bell, and one more return. If you pray, you can let each return carry Shiva's name, or the name of God you use. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson two: upavasa, the fast, which clears space and turns every pang of hunger into a bell that calls you back.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Today, the next time hunger or a craving rings, ask once: what am I here for? Then answer it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Hindus who fast on Maha Shivaratri keep different vows: some take only water, some take fruit, milk and special fasting foods such as sago, and the fast is usually broken the next morning after worship.
